# Roadmap

The core loop is finished: a human, a CPU and a training policy all play the
same engine through one seam, every shipped deck is implemented card for card,
the client runs on a desktop, a Steam Deck and a phone, and the site and the
Deck release themselves from every merge that ships. This page is what comes
after. It is the one page under `docs/` about things that do not exist yet,
and it breaks the house rule against numbers exactly where a target *is* a
number.

It is generated. Each item is a file under `docs/roadmap/` with a small front
matter and three sections, written by `/plan-feature` and worked by
`/extend-roadmap`; `scripts/roadmap.py` validates the files, derives the
grid and the queue, and writes this page. Edit the item, not the page.

How to read it:

- Each item says what is true today, what would change and how it would be
  built, and what gate would hold it. Where an item turns on a decision with
  consequences, it is marked **ADR first** and the decision gets an ADR before
  the code.
- Every item opens with three properties. **Effort** uses the sizes
  [TECH_DEBT.md](../TECH_DEBT.md) uses: **S** an afternoon, **M** a focused
  pull request, **L** a multi-PR effort; a *continuous* item is never done,
  only advanced one batch at a time. **Impact** is who it reaches and how
  often: **high** touches every game or every player of the site, **medium**
  touches a class of players or removes a weekly annoyance, **low** is polish
  somebody would notice and nobody would miss. **Depends on** names the items
  that have to land first; "nothing" means it can start today.
- An item may close with **Decisions**, the owner's answers to the questions
  its plan leaves open, and **Open questions**, the ones still waiting. An item
  with the first and not the second is decided, and only a decided item is
  built unattended ([ADR 0026](adr/0026-the-roadmap-autopilot-merges-on-green.md));
  the rest say **Awaiting decisions**.
- An item leaves this page the way a debt item leaves
  [TECH_DEBT.md](../TECH_DEBT.md): when the work lands, retire the item in the
  same pull request (`scripts/roadmap.py --done <id>`), which also unblocks
  whatever depended on it, and let the docs it touched carry the result.
  Nothing here is a changelog.

## Operating the site

### Gate the debug endpoint

Effort **S** · Impact **medium**, a hidden-information leak that is harmless until strangers share a table · Depends on nothing · Awaiting decisions.

#### Today

`GET /api/games/{id}/debug` reveals every hand on the hosted site to anyone
holding a `game_id`. It is `SV-01` in [TECH_DEBT.md](../TECH_DEBT.md), the
cheapest item there, and nothing in `server/routes.py` gates it: no setting,
mode or environment check. Nothing in the client, the desktop shell or
`scripts/` calls it; two server tests do, `test_api.py` and
`test_multiplayer_game.py`, each asserting it reveals what `player_view`
hides. `ServerSettings.mode` is `desktop` or `hosted` and nothing else, and
`ServerSettings()` defaults to `hosted`, so every `create_app` a test builds
and a local `uvicorn` run are hosted too: there is no development mode to
check for.

#### The change

Refuse it unless the app runs in a development or desktop mode;
`settings.py` already distinguishes hosted from desktop, so this is one
check in the handler. It should land before anything that puts more
strangers at one table. Delete the debt entry in the same pull request.

#### Gate

A server test that builds the app with the hosted settings and asserts the
route returns a 404, beside the existing test that asserts the desktop mode
still reveals what `player_view` hides.

#### Open questions

- **What does "development" mean, when no such mode exists?** Recommended: a
  new `ServerSettings.debug_endpoint` flag, read by `settings_from_env` from
  `COMMANDERBLITZ_DEBUG_ENDPOINT=1`, on by default when `mode` is `desktop`
  and off when it is `hosted`. A third `Mode` would change what the client is
  told by `GET /api/config` for a flag only the server reads; a flag keeps
  `mode` meaning where the server runs.
- **Does the desktop keep it?** The desktop's games are local to the
  sidecar, so nobody else holds their `game_id`. Recommended: yes, on by
  default there, so the item's "desktop still reveals" test stays true without
  an environment variable.
- **What happens to the two existing tests, whose clients are hosted?**
  Recommended: build those clients with the flag on and keep their
  assertions, and add the hosted-404 test beside each, for a single-player
  game and for a dealt pod, so both regimes in `_authorise` are covered.
- **Gate the route, or delete it?** Nothing calls it. Recommended: gate it;
  it is the one way to read a hidden zone while debugging the engine through
  the server, and deleting it would also delete the tests that hold the
  separation between `full_view` and `player_view`.
- **A check in the handler, or a route registered only when allowed?**
  Recommended: the check in the handler against `app.state.settings`, raising
  the same 404 an unknown game gets, so the route table is one fixed list and
  the refusal tells a stranger nothing.
- **Which docs move with it?** Recommended: delete `SV-01` and its line in
  the ordering at the top of `TECH_DEBT.md`, rewrite the `/debug` section of
  [server.md](server.md) to name the flag, and change the row in
  [api.md](api.md) from "development only" to the flag's name, all in the
  same pull request.

### Outcomes as data

Effort **M** · Impact **medium**, nothing a player sees, and everything brackets, matchmaking and the CPU need to be tuned from real play · Depends on nothing · Awaiting decisions.

#### Today

Several items want to know what actually happens at the table: how long
games run, which decks win, how often a draw is a `RulesLoopError`, how often
a seat is abandoned. `/health` counts live games and nothing else, and the
arena is the only source of outcomes, which measures the CPU against itself.

#### The change

One structured log line per game end, carrying deck ids, seats, turns, the
outcome and its reason, and never a name or a token; and one per
abandonment. Written by `GameSession` at the moment it already emits
`GAME_OVER`, read by nothing in the request path, and rotated by the
container's log driver as every other line is. Opt-in on the desktop, where
the player's machine is the server and the line would otherwise go nowhere.
A small script under `scripts/` folds a log into the per-deck table the
arena already prints, so the two can be read side by side.

#### Gate

A server test that plays a game to its end and asserts one line with the
documented fields and nothing identifying; the scripts table in
[scripts.md](scripts.md) gains the folding script's row.

## Presentation and branding

### A mark, a wordmark, and the surfaces that carry them

Effort **M** · Impact **medium**, the first impression for a stranger; nothing for the games already being played · Depends on nothing · Awaiting decisions.

#### Today

The door's room art, the Steam capsule and hero and the OG card all exist and
are drawn from the same scene, and the board's look is settled by
[ADR 0011](adr/0011-the-card-is-the-illustration.md): the card is the
illustration, and type is never carried by colour. What is missing is an
identity that holds at every size the project needs: a mark that survives a
favicon and a Steam library icon, a wordmark for the door and the README, and
the rule for how each sits over art it must not fight.

#### The change

- The mark and wordmark as SVG under `frontend/public/`, with the Steam
  assets regenerated from them by `frontend/scripts/make-icons.mjs` rather
  than drawn again.
- A short `docs/brand.md` naming the type pair, the signal tokens already in
  `theme.css` that the brand may use, and where the mark may and may not sit
  (never over a card face).
- The splash the desktop shell shows until the sidecar prints READY, the
  game-over screen and the not-found screen, which are the three places a
  player looks at nothing but the brand.
- Store-page material in the README: screenshots per layout mode and a short
  capture of a turn, since the Steam Deck install is the project's front door
  for a stranger.

#### Gate

The icon script regenerates every raster from the one SVG with no hand-drawn
file left in `frontend/public/`; the three brand-only screens have stories
under both layout modes; and the legibility spec covers the wordmark
wherever it sits over art.

### Sound

Effort **S** · Impact **low**, a nicer beat, in a game that already narrates every one · Depends on nothing · Awaiting decisions.

#### Today

`audio/sfx.ts` synthesises its palette at runtime, one cue per beat the
narration names, and the reduced-motion channel decides whether a cue plays.

#### The change

A recorded set with the same cue names replaces the synthesis without
touching the scheduler or the narration queue; the mute setting and the
reduced-motion channel keep their meaning. Files ship under
`frontend/public/` and count toward the content package's size budget.

#### Gate

The timing test still holds every golden batch at or under its cost, since a
cue that waits on a file load would be a lag the narration must never have;
and the mute setting's e2e assertion still passes.

## Decks

### Every precon native, one at a time, then every import

Effort **L, continuous** · Impact **high**, each precon is a shelf row a player expects, and every list a player pastes is the same card work one deck at a time · Depends on nothing.

#### Today

The manifest, `data/decks/sources.json`, lists every official Commander
precon inside the window `scripts/sync_precons.py` names as one constant.
A precon whose deck file loads ships; every other row is a coming-soon shell
on the shelf, served by `GET /api/precons/upcoming` until its deck file
loads. The cards a row lacks are `sync_precons.py --missing <id>`, and the
cards already attempted are gap records in `data/authoring/gaps/`, each
naming the capability it waits on, so `docs/unsupported-cards.md` ranks
those capabilities. A whole set at a time proved the wrong unit: Foundations
Commander's decks need dozens of capabilities between them, while one deck
needed five.

Everything that is not a shipped deck imports as a proxy that keeps its
keywords and loses its text ([deck-import.md](deck-import.md)). The loop
that closes the gap is in place: the template tier, the agent tier behind
six gates, gap records, and `/extend-dsl` to clear them
([card-authoring.md](card-authoring.md)). The queue is ordered by what
players have imported and then by EDHREC rank. Working that queue top down
spreads each batch across thousands of unrelated cards, so no batch ever
finishes a deck a player can pick.

#### The change

**One batch is one precon taken to 100%.** The batch is the manifest row
fewest cards short of native, newest first among equals; a row whose
missing cards have never been through the queue goes through
`/author-cards` by name first, because until it has, its distance is
unknown. The batch:

1. Runs `/author-cards` by name over the row's `--missing` list, which
   either writes a card or files its gap record.
2. Clears every capability those gap records name, one `/extend-dsl` run
   and one commit per capability, in the order the most cards elsewhere in
   the catalog wait on it. A capability that needs a rules subsystem the
   engine does not have ([rules-coverage.md](rules-coverage.md#not-implemented))
   stops the batch: it becomes its own item and the precon waits on it.
3. Re-authors the row's cards until `--missing` is empty, then
   `--write-deck` writes the deck file with its printings and release. A
   person writes the dossier and picks an `archetype`, and the deck joins
   `PRECONS` in `tests/cards/test_deck_legality.py`, which puts it under the
   import pin and the sampled whole-game test. Its shell disappears by
   itself.
4. Harvests the rest of the catalog the batch's capabilities unblocked: the
   template tier with `--retry`, then one `/author-cards` wave over the
   pending cards the new vocabulary reaches.

A deck gets a strategy module and a page under `docs/cpus/` only where its
archetype visibly misplays it. A row the window ages out is the script
reporting a precon to retire, and its deck leaves the shelf in the same
batch.

**After the window.** Once every row in the window is native, the unit stays
a deck: the most-imported public list that is not native, then the next
older precon. The target is unchanged: any public Moxfield link a player
pastes imports with a simplified count of zero, and keeps doing so as sets
are released. A set release is a manifest refresh, which makes the new
precons the next batches before players meet the cards; the gap report
after each release is the list of mechanics the set introduced.

**What the catalog runs into, in the order it will be met:**

1. **The validator.** Every new op adds a branch to `_validate_effect`, which
   is already the largest function in the tree (`OF-01` in
   [TECH_DEBT.md](../TECH_DEBT.md)). A per-op validator registry,
   mirroring the engine's `@register`, is the precondition for the long tail.
2. **The deliberate simplifications** in
   [rules-coverage.md](rules-coverage.md#simplified): layers-lite
   ([ADR 0001](adr/0001-layers-lite.md)) once two statics genuinely depend
   on each other, card-level targets chosen before modes, and the absence of
   a general replacement system. Each of these is an ADR amendment, not a
   card.
3. **The not-implemented list** in the same page: each is additive and each
   is ordered by how many cards the gap report says it blocks.
4. **Test cost.** `test_every_card_works` and the auto-card gates run over
   the whole pool on every run; at the catalog's size the python slice needs
   sharding by card file, and the golden pool hash a per-file variant.
5. **Art.** Every supported card wants its illustration, which is the art
   store.

This item is continuous: `/extend-roadmap` takes one precon of it and
leaves the item on the page.

#### Gate

Per batch: `tests/cards/test_precon_imports.py` over the new deck; one unit
test per capability under `tests/unit/`; the manifest test (every row inside
the window, every `precon` deck has a row) and the coming-soon test
(`tests/server/test_upcoming_precons.py`) still green; and the sampled
whole-game test able to draw the new deck. Across batches,
`author_cards.py --report` for coverage and the generated
[unsupported-cards.md](unsupported-cards.md) for what blocks what.

### Viewing a deck's list

Effort **M** · Impact **medium**, every deck pick, and the only honest per-card view of an import · Depends on nothing · Awaiting decisions.

#### Today

The dossier shows the commander, the editorial half, the curve, the
land count and the simplified count. It never shows the list, so the only
way to know what is in a deck is to deal it, and the only way to know
*which* of an import's cards are inert is the import report at the moment
of import.

#### The change

A list view, the way Moxfield's default view reads: every card as a
face, grouped by type with the group counts, sorted by mana value within a
group, with `Y` or hover reading the card in full through the same preview
the board uses. Specifics:

- A new `GET /api/decks/{id}/cards` rather than widening `DeckDetail`, which
  is fetched for every dossier and should stay light; the list is derived at
  request time like the curve, so it cannot drift from the file.
- A **per-card** simplified marker, so an imported deck says which cards are
  inert rather than only how many; the coverage file the importer writes
  already knows.
- Where the source list carries the author's categories, keep them on the
  import and offer "by category" beside "by type"; where it does not, "by
  type" is the only grouping and nothing is invented.
- A stats strip: the curve that exists, colour pips against mana sources,
  type counts, and the bracket signals once brackets exist. Charts
  follow the dataviz rules the project already uses for the curve, in both
  themes.
- `StaticCard` for every face, since a second `layoutId` for an oid would
  animate between copies, and group headers as regions so the ring walks a
  hundred cards by group rather than one at a time.

The same view is what a seat opens in the pod to check an opponent's locked
deck, so it has to render for a deck with no dossier at all. It is worth
more once the precons exist, but nothing in it waits on them.

#### Gate

A server test that the new route's groups sum to the deck's card count and
its per-card markers agree with the coverage file; a story per layout mode
with a hundred faces under the floors; and an e2e spec that walks the list
with a pad by group and reads one card.

## Play experience

### Difficulty

Effort **S** · Impact **medium**, visible in every pod, and the place the CPU work lands where a player can see it · Depends on nothing · Awaiting decisions.

#### Today

Three agents already exist with a clear ordering: `heuristic_classic`,
`heuristic` with its strategies, and `policy`, all built by `agent_by_name`.
The wire already carries a per-seat agent: `SeatConfig.agent` and
`SeatAdminRequest.agent` accept `random`, `heuristic` or `policy`, and the
lobby's `set_agent` seat action stores it. Nothing in the client sends it:
`PodRoute` calls `adminSeat` only for the actions without an agent, so every
CPU a player seats plays `heuristic`. `heuristic_classic` is not a value the
server accepts, and `GameSession` builds every agent without a checkpoint, so
`policy` is `PolicyAgent` falling back to the heuristic. No checkpoint ships,
and [ai-training.md](ai-training.md) trains one per pod size.

#### The change

A per-seat choice in the pod (easy, normal, hard) as a field on `SeatConfig`
and a segment on the CPU chair, mapped to the three agents, with hard meaning
the best checkpoint shipped and falling back to the strategy CPU when none
is. It gives the learned-judgement work a place to land that a player can
see, and it ships before any model does.

#### Gate

The lobby's predicates in `logic/lobby.ts` cover the new field; the pod
server tests assert the agent each seat is dealt; and the lobby story and
e2e spec reach the segment with a pad under the floors.

#### Open questions

- **A new field, or the existing `agent`?** The change names a field on
  `SeatConfig`, but `agent` and `set_agent` are already that seam end to end.
  Recommended: keep `agent` as the one field and map easy, normal and hard
  onto it in the client, adding `heuristic_classic` to the accepted values;
  a second field that only translates to the first is two sources for one
  fact.
- **What is easy?** Recommended: `heuristic_classic`, the agent from before
  strategies, not `random`, which makes no game of it; `random` stays a value
  the API takes and the segment does not offer.
- **Where does the hard checkpoint live, and how is it found?** None ships
  today, and one is trained per pod size. Recommended: build the seam only,
  a server setting naming a checkpoint per pod size that `GameSession` hands
  to a `policy` seat, unset by default so hard plays the strategy CPU; which
  checkpoint ships, and whether it is committed or deployed beside the site,
  is a later item with its own ADR.
- **Does hard say it is falling back?** With no checkpoint, hard and normal
  play the same game. Recommended: keep all three segments and let the seat
  report the agent it actually got, so the lobby can mark hard as "strategy
  CPU" until a model lands, rather than hiding the segment.
- **Who may set it?** Recommended: the host, through `set_agent`, the same
  rule as the seat's deck; a joined player's own seat is human and has no
  difficulty.
- **Does a rematch keep it?** `GameRoute`'s rematch rebuilds the seats
  through `useNewGame` and omits `agent`, because the table view does not say
  which agent a seat runs, so every rematch plays `heuristic`. Recommended:
  the player view carries each CPU seat's agent and the rematch sends it back,
  so a hard table stays hard, in the same pull request.

### The stack reads in order from the panel

Effort **S** · Impact **medium**, every response to a response, which is the skill the format is about · Depends on nothing · Awaiting decisions.

#### Today

`StackPanel` draws the stack as a pile of faces, top first, with the
targeting relationship drawn by `CombatArrows`; a press on a ply is a target
when a spell is waiting for one and otherwise a read
(`useTableGestures.onStackItem`). At the handheld size the pile is a rail
panel the ring can land on but cannot read in order: a stack of three is
three faces offset by `PLY_Y`, the two below the top are mostly covered, and
the only text that says what resolves next is on the face itself. The
action panel, which is the one surface every decision can be answered from
([ADR 0015](adr/0015-every-legal-action-is-one-control.md)), says nothing
about the stack at all: a priority window with three items on the stack is
drawn the same as one with none, so the player responding to a response
reads the order off a pile of art.

#### The change

The panel is the one place the stack is read in order, and the pile is the
picture of it.

- **A stack strip in the panel.** While `state.stack` is non-empty on a
  priority window, the panel's head carries one line per item, top first,
  in the words the log already uses for the same item (`logic/events.ts`
  names a stack item the way the ticker does), each naming its controller
  and its targets, with "resolves next" on the first. Lines, not stops: the
  strip is read, and the pile remains the thing to press.
- **The pile stays the pile.** `StackPanel` is unchanged except that
  pressing a ply while nothing is being targeted sends the ring to the
  strip's matching line, so a controller can read a buried item without
  uncovering it.
- **Nothing changes size with game state**
  ([ADR 0016](adr/0016-nothing-changes-size-with-game-state.md)): the
  strip is a fixed number of lines, and a stack deeper than that scrolls
  inside it rather than growing the panel.

What it does not do: change what the engine puts on the stack, or add an
action. A response is still the cast or activate action the panel already
carries.

#### Gate

A `StackPanel` story and a panel story with a stack of three, each at the
handheld floors, asserting the strip reads top first and that the panel's
box is the same height as with an empty stack. A journey in
`Journeys.stories.tsx` that responding to a response costs no more presses
than responding to a spell, under the priority row's ceiling in
`decisionAudit.ts`.

#### Open questions

- **Today no longer matches the code: the pile is not a rail panel.**
  `TablePlay` floats `StackPanel` over the play area at every size, in the
  grid cell `.play__mine` sits in, and the pile is only drawn while
  `state.stack` is non-empty. Each ply already wears a tag reading "next",
  "ability" and its controller's name; only the targets are missing as text
  (they are in `data-hint`, and drawn by `CombatArrows`). The
  `[data-compact] .rail--right .stackpanel` cap in `styles/handheld.css` styles
  a placement that no longer exists. Recommended: proceed on these facts,
  rewrite **Today** to match in the decide commit, and delete the dead
  handheld rule in the pull request, since the strip replaces what it was
  for.
- **Where do the strip's words come from?** `logic/events.ts` names no stack
  item: the log's words are `describeEvent` in `logic/labels.ts`, which names
  a `spell_cast` or `ability_triggered` event rather than a `StackItemView`,
  and `ActionPanel` already resolves a `stack` target ref to the item's name.
  Recommended: one pure `stackLine(state, item)` in `logic/labels.ts` beside
  `describeEvent`, reusing its name and target lookups and verb agreement
  (`You` for the viewer), with a unit test, so the strip and the log cannot
  drift apart; `StackPanel`'s own target string moves onto it too.
- **How many lines, and what fills the box when the stack is empty?**
  ADR 0016 reserves a slot at its full size, and the gate asserts the panel's
  box is the same height with and without a stack, but the strip shows only
  "while `state.stack` is non-empty". Recommended: three lines, drawn in
  `.acts__head` below the prompt on every priority window, reading `—` when the
  stack is empty, with `scrollbar-gutter: stable` and an inside scroll beyond
  three, so the strip's height is a constant and `.acts__list` never moves.
  The alternative, taking the strip's height out of `.acts__list` only while
  the stack is non-empty, keeps the box but moves every action under the ring.
- **Only on priority windows, or on every decision while the stack is
  non-empty?** A target pick for a counterspell, or a trigger's choice, is
  made with the stack in play too. Recommended: every decision while the stack
  is non-empty draws the strip, and every decision reserves its slot, since a
  slot that appears on some decision kinds and not others is the same jump
  ADR 0016 forbids.
- **"Lines, not stops", yet a ply press "sends the ring to the strip's
  line".** The ring can only stand on a stop, and a ply press outside
  targeting already opens the item in the reader (`holdCard` in
  `useTableGestures.onStackItem`), which reads a buried item without
  uncovering it. Recommended: keep the lines non-stops and keep the press a
  read; the press also marks the matching line (`aria-current`) while the
  reader is up, rather than moving the ring, so ADR 0015's one-control rule is
  untouched and the change to `StackPanel` is a highlight.
- **Which journey, and what is its ceiling?** `BUDGET` in `decisionAudit.ts`
  has no response journey; the priority row is held to `PassInOnePress` and
  `AimASpell`. Recommended: a new `RespondToAResponse` journey in
  `Journeys.stories.tsx`, on a stack of two with a counterspell in hand aimed
  at the top item, with the ceiling `AimASpell` already holds (the card, then
  the target), added to the priority row's `journeys`.
- **The phone?** On a phone the right rail is a sheet holding `ActionPanel`
  (`TablePhone.stories.tsx` holds it). Recommended:
  the strip is part of `ActionPanel`, so the phone gets it with no extra work;
  the gate adds the phone viewport to the panel story rather than a separate
  phone story.

### Why a press is refused

Effort **S** · Impact **medium**, every player who presses a permanent that does nothing and has to guess why · Depends on nothing · Awaiting decisions.

#### Today

Two of the three refusals a player meets already carry the engine's own
reason. A hand card that cannot be played arrives with one of
`UnplayableReason` in `PlayerView.hand_reasons`, from
`legality.unplayable_reason`, and `HandFan` draws it: priority, timing, the
land drop, mana, no legal target. A card that cannot be *targeted* carries
`LegalAction.untargetable` from the same `target_refusal` that
`can_be_targeted` answers with, and `logic/targetHint.ts` turns it into one
sentence in the foot. The third refusal is silent: a permanent whose
activated ability cannot be activated now (a tap ability on a tapped or
summoning-sick creature, a cost the pool cannot pay, a loyalty ability
already used this turn, a cast lock) is pressable and does nothing, and
`logic/abilities.ts` can only say that no `activate` action names it.

#### The change

The same hint, for the same reasons, on a permanent. The engine already
decides every one of these refusals in `legality`; this item surfaces the
decision it made rather than re-deriving one in the client
([architecture.md](architecture.md)).

- **The engine says why.** `PlayerView` gains `ability_reasons`, keyed by
  oid, built beside `hand_reasons` in `serialize.player_view` from a
  `legality.unactivatable_reason` that answers in the vocabulary
  `unplayable_reason` already uses, extended by the two reasons only an
  ability has: tapped (or summoning sick, for a tap cost) and already
  activated this turn. Only for the viewer's own permanents, and only the
  gates that are closed, so a permanent absent from the map is activatable
  and the map is empty on most boards.
- **The foot says it.** `targetHint` grows a sibling in `logic/` that reads
  `ability_reasons` for the hovered or ringed permanent while nothing is
  being targeted, in the sentence shape `targetHint` uses, and the foot's
  hint draws it as a refusal. `HandFan`'s reason rendering and this one read
  one label table in `logic/labels.ts`, so the same gate says the same thing
  from either zone.

What it does not do: offer an action that was not legal, or change what a
press on a refused permanent does. Pressing it still reads the card.

#### Gate

An engine test per reason in `tests/unit/` that `unactivatable_reason`
names it and that an activatable permanent is absent from the map; a server
test that an opponent's seat gets `null`. `tests/targetHint.test.ts`'s
sibling for the new hint, one case per reason, and that it is silent while
targeting. A story in `HintBar.stories.tsx` or `TableFoot`'s nearest that
draws the refusal at the handheld floors.

### CPU takeover and reconnection

Effort **M** · Impact **medium**, every multi-human game somebody drops from; required before strangers share a table · Depends on nothing · Awaiting decisions.

#### Today

A seat whose human stops answering holds the table. The pod sweep already
evicts an idle chair before the deal; after it, the sweep ends the whole
session when it goes idle, and there is no middle state. Rejoining with the
same token is already the reconnect story, so a player who comes back finds
their seat if the game is still there, and nothing if it is not.

#### The change

Once sessions persist, a seat idle past a threshold is piloted by the
strategy CPU for the deck it holds, the human may reclaim it with the same
token, and the table is told both times. The threshold is a constant on
`GameSession` beside the TTLs, the takeover is the existing `drive_ai` over
one more seat, and the handback is one tape entry that records the switch so
undo and replay see it. The pod view and the game view each carry the seat's
state, so an orb can say "away". This is the precondition for matchmaking
with strangers, where leaving is normal.

#### Gate

A multiplayer server test that lets one seat go idle, asserts the CPU acts
for it and the others are told, then rejoins with the token and asserts the
human is back in control with the tape intact; and the pod e2e spec driving
two browsers through the same.

### Replays and sharing

Effort **M** · Impact **medium**, every bug report becomes a tape and every CPU misplay becomes a training position · Depends on nothing · Awaiting decisions.

#### Today

The seed and the tape are a replay ([ADR 0005](adr/0005-no-state-cloning.md)),
and undo already rebuilds a game from them, but nothing exposes them: a game
ends and its tape goes with the session, so a bug seen at the table cannot be
handed to anybody, and a CPU misplay cannot be pointed at by the arena.

#### The change

A "share this game" link that serves the seed and the tape to a replay
viewer. The viewer is the existing table in a read-only mode, stepping the
narration beat by beat with the playback controls that already exist, with
every seat's hand hidden as `player_view` hides it today unless the sharer
chose to reveal their own. A tape file is also what a bug report attaches
and what `run_arena.py` accepts as a starting position, so a misplay seen
once becomes a seeded test. Persisted sessions make the tape durable past
the game; this item makes it a URL.

#### Gate

A server test that a shared tape replays to the same final state and the
same event log as the game that produced it; a client test that the viewer
sends no action; and the arena accepting a tape as a position under test.

### Archidekt import

Effort **S** · Impact **low**, the second link players paste; the maintainer pastes the first · Depends on nothing · Awaiting decisions.

#### Today

Only a Moxfield link imports. [deck-import.md](deck-import.md) already
says a second site is an adapter, not a second card pipeline: what a card
*is* comes from the catalog, and the source supplies only names, quantities
and printings.

#### The change

An Archidekt adapter beside `moxfield.py` with the same signature, the URL
parser deciding which one a pasted link goes to, and the same error codes.
Printings are carried through where the source names them, as the Moxfield
adapter does.

#### Gate

A test with a real, trimmed Archidekt payload beside `moxfield_deck.json`,
run through `importer.import_deck` as a dry run, asserting the same cards
resolve the same way as the equivalent Moxfield list.

## The Steam Deck build

### Compressed art, shipped for offline precon play

Effort **M** · Impact **medium**, every Deck update gets smaller and every precon plays offline from the first launch · Depends on nothing · Awaiting decisions.

#### Today

The content package the Deck downloads carries the frozen server,
the built client and the card data as one versioned asset, and the art the
repository commits rides inside it at the size the site serves. Anything
outside the shipped pool is fetched on first sight, or eagerly on import,
and only while online ([steamdeck.md](steamdeck.md#offline-and-online)). So
the Deck's offline promise is exactly as wide as the art it holds, and
every content update re-downloads illustrations that did not change.

#### The change

A second encoding of the art, made for the device, shipped
with the precons, and versioned apart from the code:

- **One encoding per surface.** The Deck's panel is a fixed size and the
  largest card it ever draws is the full-card read, so a modern format at
  that width, and the board width beside it, is a fraction of the site's
  bytes with no visible loss on the panel. The rule of
  [ADR 0012](adr/0012-art-fetched-once-served-locally.md) holds unchanged:
  nothing is ever upscaled, which is exactly why the encoding is sized to
  the largest the Deck draws and not smaller.
- **The art store makes it.** The backfill job writes the device
  encoding beside the full one, keyed the same way, so the site serves
  `/art/...` at either size on request and the sidecar asks for the small
  one. One crawl, two outputs, no second source.
- **The precon window ships inside the package**, so every deck on the
  shelf plays offline with its art on the first launch; everything a player
  imports arrives through the complete-imports item.
- **Art is its own asset.** `content-latest.json` grows an art version, the
  release carries `art-<v>` beside `content-<v>`, and the updater fetches the
  art asset only when its version moved. Code ships on every merge; art
  ships when a set is added to the window or a pin changes. A content update
  gets small enough to take over a hotel connection, which is where a Deck
  usually is.

The licensing ADR the art store forces covers this too: a second encoding
is the same illustration, and the decision is about what is distributed,
not at which size.

#### Gate

`e2e/legibility.spec.ts` runs against the compressed set under the handheld
project, so the scrims and the text are proven over the bytes the device
will actually show. The package and the art asset each get a ceiling in the
release workflow, in the spirit of
[ADR 0013](adr/0013-handheld-floors-are-ci-gates.md): a precon set that
would push the asset over its budget fails the release rather than quietly
doubling every Deck's download. The desktop updater's unit tests cover an
art version that moved and one that did not.

### Site imports follow their owner to the Deck

Effort **M** · Impact **medium**, a deck imported on the site with friends is on the Deck the next time its owner plays alone · Depends on nothing · Awaiting decisions.

#### Today

A deck reaches the site from the Deck through the hand-off: the
Online card carries the Moxfield ids of the decks imported at home
(`onlineUrl` in `frontend/src/logic/desktop.ts`) and `HomeRoute`'s hand-off
imports them before showing the door. Nothing goes the other way, which
[ADR 0009](adr/0009-offline-first-desktop.md) records as a consequence:
a deck imported on the site does not come back. The two ends do not even
agree on who the owner is. A library is a random id each client mints into
its own `localStorage` (`frontend/src/state/library.ts`), and the site's
browser and the Deck's window are two clients with two ids, so the site has
no way to know that a deck its browser library imported belongs to the
player holding a given Deck. The half that exists is the other direction's
plumbing ([ADR 0022](adr/0022-deck-imports-through-the-site.md)): a Deck's
own import goes through the site under the Deck's library id, comes back
through `GET /api/decks/{deck_id}/bundle` and `adopt_bundle`, and is finished
by `POST /api/decks/complete` at the door.

#### The change

A deck imported on the site is on its owner's Deck after the
next launch with a connection, complete, through the bundle route, the
adopt step and the `complete` verdict that already exist, unchanged.

- **One library across the hand-off.** The Online hand-off carries the
  Deck's library id, and the site's client adopts it for that browser
  session rather than its own, so whatever the player imports there is
  stamped with the Deck's id. A browser with a library of its own keeps it;
  this changes only a window the Deck opened.
- **The Deck asks what it is missing.** A route on the site lists the decks
  a library owns with their Moxfield ids; at launch with a connection, the
  same step that finishes incomplete decks adopts any the Deck lacks, through
  the bundle, before the door.
- It does not merge two libraries that already exist, or add accounts.

#### Gate

A server test lists a library's decks on the site and
nobody else's. The desktop entry point's tests import a deck on a stub site
under the Deck's library, relaunch the sidecar, and assert the deck is on
disk and complete. A client test holds that a window opened by the hand-off
adopts the Deck's library id and an ordinary browser keeps its own.

## Advanced CPUs

### Learned judgements behind the strategy hooks

Effort **L** · Impact **high**, every game the maintainer plays is against the CPU, and so is most of every stranger's first · Depends on [Outcomes as data](#outcomes-as-data), [Replays and sharing](#replays-and-sharing), [Difficulty](#difficulty) · Awaiting decisions.

#### Today

The CPU is reflexive: the heuristic scores every legal action from
the position in front of it and a per-deck `Strategy` adjusts the scores
([cpus/README.md](cpus/README.md)). It cannot look ahead, because state is
never cloned, and it reads the table only as board power and life. The gaps a
playtester notices are the ones [TECH_DEBT.md](../TECH_DEBT.md) lists under
"Strategy gaps" and the ones the CPU page admits: it attacks whoever is
softest rather than whoever is winning, points removal by printed size rather
than by what a permanent is doing, and never holds mana open on purpose.

The trainer exists ([ai-training.md](ai-training.md)): masked PPO over a
structured action space, a per-card embedding, a snapshot pool of opponents,
and an arena that reports win rates with confidence intervals. What it has
not been given is enough experience, and a whole-policy replacement of the
heuristic is a long road for a reward that arrives once per game.

#### The change

**Learn the judgements, keep the plan.** The strategy
hooks are already the seams where the CPU's judgement enters: `defender`,
`attack_value`, `block_value`, `priority_value`, `choose`, `junk_value`. Each
takes the agent's answer and returns the one to use. A learned model can sit
behind any of them, trained from the same environment, while the deck plan
goes on deciding what the deck is trying to do. Three models, in the order
they pay off:

1. **Threat.** Which seat is winning, and which permanent on the table is
   doing the most for its controller. Trained as a value head from self-play
   outcomes and from the outcome log the site will keep: the input is the
   observation the environment already encodes plus the card embeddings, the
   target is who went on to win. It feeds `defender` (attack the seat that is
   ahead, not the one that is low), the removal half of `priority_value`
   (point the Swords at the engine, not the biggest body), and the
   counterspell rule (hold it for the spell that matters).
2. **Tempo.** Whether to spend mana now or keep it up: a classifier over the
   same observation that predicts whether a held instant is used profitably
   before the CPU's next turn. This is the "hold mana open" gap, and it
   changes only the ordering `priority_value` returns.
3. **Combat.** `logic/fight.ts` and `board.could_block` model a fight one
   pair at a time; a learned block and attack valuation over the whole
   declaration is the piece the reflexive agent cannot do by rule.

Each model is a few hundred kilobytes and runs under the same mask, so the
CPU can never pick an illegal action and the structural guarantees of the
single seam are untouched. Each ships as a checkpoint the `policy` agent
already knows how to load, under the difficulty picker.

**Where lookahead fits.** [ADR 0005](adr/0005-no-state-cloning.md) rules out
cloning in the engine; it does not rule out *replay* as a way to explore a
line offline. A search agent that forks the tape, replays, and scores the
result is affordable for generating training positions, where wall-clock
does not matter, and not for play, where it does. So the search exists to
teach the models, and the models play. This is the one place the no-cloning
decision is worth re-reading before work starts; it does not need amending.

Deliver it one model at a time, the threat model first, each as its own
pull request with its own arena result in the body.

#### Gate

The arena with the deck held fixed and only the pilot swapped is the sharp
test: the threat model's first gate is that the strategy CPU with it beats
the strategy CPU without it on every precon at a confidence the arena
reports, and that the draw rate does not move. Each of the strategy gaps in
the debt page becomes a seeded position in `tests/ai/strategy/` that the new
pilot must get right. The baseline heuristic stays the opponent `verify.py`
gates on until a checkpoint has beaten it across the board for long enough
to be trusted.

## Matchmaking

### Brackets, derived from the list

Effort **M** · Impact **medium**, a filter and a signal on every tile; the precondition for the queue · Depends on nothing · Awaiting decisions.

#### Today

Nothing on a tile or in a dossier says how strong a deck is beyond the
editorial ratings a person wrote for a shipped deck, and an import has none.
The Commander Brackets, one to five, are defined by what a list contains:
Game Changers, mass land denial, chained extra turns, two-card infinite
combos, and tutors, with the thresholds per bracket set by the format's own
rules and revised by its stewards from time to time.

#### The change

Most of a bracket can be read off a deck at request time, beside the curve,
so it cannot drift:

- a hand-kept `data/catalog/game_changers.json`, with the same discipline as
  `art_pins.json`: a named list, a test that every entry resolves in the
  catalog, and a note on where the list comes from;
- counts over the list for extra turns, tutors and land destruction, from
  oracle text and the engine's own vocabulary where a card is native;
- a hand-kept table of two-card combos, from the community's combo database,
  which the arena can go on to verify as the pairs become native.

The derived bracket is a suggestion, because the format defines a bracket as
a conversation, not a measurement, and an editorial `bracket` on a shipped
deck overrides it where the heuristic misreads a list. It is shown on the
tile and in the dossier, filters the shelf, and is what the queue matches
on. It waits on the precon data model because the deck file's fields and
the shelf's filters are settled there.

#### Gate

A test that every Game Changer and every combo entry resolves in the
catalog; `deckinfo.py` tests pinning the bracket each shipped deck derives;
and the shelf's filter in a story and the e2e catalogue spec.

### A queue

Effort **L** · Impact **medium**, strangers only, and the site is mostly one player today · Depends on [CPU takeover and reconnection](#cpu-takeover-and-reconnection), [Brackets, derived from the list](#brackets-derived-from-the-list), [Outcomes as data](#outcomes-as-data) · Awaiting decisions.

#### Today

A pod is reached by a code read down a phone line, so a table is only ever
people who already know each other. There is no way to be paired with a
stranger, and nothing that would make such a pairing fair.

#### The change

**Shape.** `POST /api/queue {deck_id, pod_size}` and a long poll on the ticket,
the way pods already work ([ADR 0007](adr/0007-versioned-long-polling.md)).
The server forms a pod when it holds enough compatible tickets, returns the
pod code and a player token, and from there the existing lobby and deal run
unchanged: matchmaking creates pods, it does not replace them. Compatibility
is the deck's bracket within one step, widening as a ticket ages; a ticket
older than a threshold is dealt with CPU seats rather than left waiting. The
whole feature lives on the hosted site, since the desktop already goes there
for anyone who is not on the LAN.

**What it needs first, and why each is a dependency:**

- persisted sessions and CPU takeover, because a stranger who leaves is the
  common case and a queue that produces dropped games teaches players not to
  use it;
- the outcome log, so the bracket thresholds can be tuned from games rather
  than guessed;
- an identity that outlives a pod only if anything is ever rated. Nothing in
  forming a pod needs one. A client-generated id in local storage is enough
  for "do not re-pair me with the seat that just left", and real accounts are
  a separate decision with an ADR of its own, taken only when ratings or a
  history are wanted.

**Scale.** A parked thread per waiting client is the long-poll's cost, and a
queue adds waiters. That is fine at the scale the site is for, and the day it
is not is the day a second worker and a shared store are needed, which is the
real reason the persisted-session work comes first.

#### Gate

Server tests in the shape of `test_pod_races.py`: N tickets from N threads
form the right number of pods with compatible brackets and no ticket seated
twice; an aged ticket is dealt with CPUs; and a formed pod is an ordinary
pod to every existing test. The pod e2e spec drives two browsers through
the queue into one table.

## Not planned

Named so that nobody re-litigates them by accident:

- **Colour accessibility** stays out of scope
  ([ADR 0006](adr/0006-no-colour-accessibility-requirement.md)).
- **A progressive web app** and **WebSockets** were each rejected with
  reasons ([ADR 0009](adr/0009-offline-first-desktop.md),
  [ADR 0007](adr/0007-versioned-long-polling.md)); the matchmaking queue
  is the first thing that could revisit the second, and only at a scale the
  site does not yet have.
- **Non-English cards.** The catalog is built from the English bundle on
  purpose ([card-catalog.md](card-catalog.md#why-default_cards)).
- **Undo in a multiplayer game.** Refused by design
  ([api.md](api.md#undo)); a take-back by consent is a different feature and
  nobody has asked for it.
